# Selection of officials by lot (sortition) (`sortition`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by secret_ballot, public_accounts_audit
- Core idea: Offices and juries are filled by drawing lots among all qualified citizens for short terms, usually one year and not repeatable. A fair draw gives eligible citizens a chance to serve and reduces the value of campaigning. A small sample can still leave groups unrepresented. It works when tasks are done by boards rather than one man, candidates are vetted before and audited after office, and posts that need skill (generals, treasurers, engineers) are still elected. Athens, a city of some 30,000 citizens, filled most of its offices this way for nearly two centuries.
- Pitfalls:
  - Using lot for jobs that need rare skill: Athens elected its generals and financial officers
  - Lot without scrutiny before office and audit after it invites the incompetent and corrupt
  - Idealising Athens: women, slaves and resident foreigners, the large majority, had no part
- History: greece: c. 487 BC – Athenian archons chosen by lot; 5th–4th c. BC council of 500, most magistrates and all juries drawn by lot, later with the kleroterion allotment machine; india: c. 920 – Uttaramerur (Chola) inscriptions: village committee members drawn by a child from a pot of palm-leaf tickets (kudavolai), with property, age and learning qualifications and a ban on recent holders and their kin; rome: Republic – lot decides the order of voting units and the allocation of provinces, not who holds office; europe: 1268 – Venice elects its doge through alternating rounds of lot and vote; 1328 Florence draws the priors from bags of approved names (tratte) for two-month terms
- Read:
  - Mogens Herman Hansen, The Athenian Democracy in the Age of Demosthenes (1991)
  - Aristotle, Athenaion Politeia (Constitution of the Athenians), c. 330 BC
  - Bernard Manin, The Principles of Representative Government (1997)
